output.title: ICC constitutes trial chamber for Rodrigo Duterte case | ABS-CBN News
output.description: The International Criminal Court (ICC) has constituted the Trial Chamber in the case against former President Rodrigo Duterte.
output.text: A man holds a portrait of former Philippines president Rodrigo Duterte in front of the International Criminal Court (ICC) where he will be appearing, in The Hague on March 14, 2025. Nicolas Tucat, AFP/File MANILA — The International Criminal Court (ICC) has constituted the Trial Chamber in the case against former President Rodrigo Duterte. This moves the proceedings to the trial phase, after Pre-Trial Chamber I confirmed all three counts of crimes against humanity against him on April 23. In a decision dated April 24, 2026, the Presidency, composed of ICC President Tomoko Akane, First Vice-President Rosario Salvatore Aitala, and Second Vice-President Reine Alapini-Gansou, named the following judges to compose Trial Chamber III: -- Joanna Korner (United Kingdom) -- Keebong Paek (Republic of Korea) -- Nicolas Guillou (France) READ: Who are the judges in Duterte's trial at the ICC? "NOTING article 61(11) of the Statute, pursuant to which the Presidency shall constitute a Trial Chamber once the charges have been confirmed, which shall be responsible for the conduct of subsequent proceedings," the decision read. The Presidency also "DECIDES to refer the case of The Prosecutor v. Rodrigo Roa Duterte to Trial Chamber III;" formally transferring jurisdiction over the next phase of proceedings. The ICC last week announced that pre-trial judges "unanimously" confirmed crimes against humanity charges tied to Duterte's war on drugs between November 1, 2011 and March 16, 2019, covering his time as Davao City mayor and later as president. READ: Duterte to face ICC trial after judges confirm charges The Presidency ordered the ICC Registrar to transmit the full record of proceedings, including the confirmation decision, to the newly constituted chamber. It said the composition of the chamber was guided by the need to ensure "efficient management of the Court's workload," taking into account "the experience and expertise of each judge," as well as the need to expedite proceedings and balance judicial assignments. "CONSIDERING the current and anticipated overall judicial workload of the Court and the necessity to ensure sound management of the same, the need to expedite proceedings, the workload and individual concerns of the respective judges, particularly those assigned to the Trial Division, their previous involvement in cases, as well as the experience and expertise of each judge," the decision stated. With the chamber now in place, the case formally enters the trial stage, where judges will oversee proceedings, rule on evidence, and ultimately determine guilt or innocence. Duterte, 81, will be the first Asian former head of state to face trial at the ICC, which prosecutes individuals for the world's worst crimes such as war crimes and crimes against humanity. Duterte's lead counsel Nicholas Kaufman previously lamented how the credibility of the witnesses was never assessed at confirmation. READ: ICC jurisdiction decision on ‘big catch’ Duterte was expected -- Kaufman "The Pre Trial Chamber found that the crucial word 'neutralise', used to define a so-called State or organisational policy, was understood by those involved in the operations to mean to 'kill'. This is hardly surprising when the whole of the Prosecution's case, as pasted into the concluding paragraphs of the Pre-Trial Chamber's decision, is based on the uncorroborated statements of vicious self-confessed murderers acting as cooperating witnesses," he said. "At trial, the Defence will prove that the aforementioned 'State policy' is a complete fiction. The Defence will also show that the evidence of very same criminal witnesses, so gleefully peddled by the former President's many detractors, has zero weight," he added. The only time Duterte has been seen since his arrest and transfer to The Hague was at an initial appearance via videolink in March 2025. The Rome Statute, however, requires the presence of the accused during trial.

output.title: Amici curiae Panganiban, Davide, Puno: 16 votes not the required conviction threshold
output.description: Former Supreme Court chief justices Artemio Panganiban, Hilario Davide, and Reynato Puno said Wednesday the constitutional voting threshold required to convict an impeachable official should be based on the number of senator-judges who actively participated in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
output.text: Former Supreme Court (SC) chief justices Artemio Panganiban, Hilario Davide, and Reynato Puno said Wednesday the constitutional voting threshold required to convict an impeachable official should be based on the number of senator-judges who actively participated in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte. Panganiban, Davide, and Puno conveyed their positions during Day 26 of the Duterte impeachment trial, wherein amici curiae were heard by the Senate impeachment court to hear their expert views on what should be the voting threshold needed for the conviction of an impeachable official. However, former SC associate justice Adolfo Azcuna, one of the framers of the 1987 Constitution, offered a different view that the two-thirds concurrence requirement should relate to the entire membership of the Senate, hence a conviction by 16 senator-judges is needed. Panganiban said, "Active participation and independent evaluation of the evidence are essential to discharge the Senate's and the Senator's constitutional responsibility." EXPLAINER: What are amici curiae? "As the elected representatives of the Filipino people, the Senate's mandate demands a commonsensical interpretation of the Constitution. Meaningful adjudication requires active participation in the search for truth and fairness. It is only in this manner that a verdict that is fair to the parties, fair to the Senators, and ultimately fair to our sovereign people," Panganiban added. Four of the current 24 senator-judges of the vice president's trial are either detained for plunder cases or remain in hiding. Davide, for his part, said the framers of the 1987 Constitution setting the threshold to convict on the basis of two thirds of all members of the Senate did not intend to include those physically incapacitated, charged with plunder and corruption cases, or in hiding due to legal impediments. "We have decisions of the Supreme Court which clearly decree that public officers facing criminal cases in court cannot, during the pendency of their cases, practice their profession nor hold office, elective or appointive while in detention. Clearly then, the basis of computing the two thirds must be the number of senators who are qualified to vote, not the 24 in the present Senate," Davide said in his written position read by the Clerk of Court Renato Bantug. "All those disqualified by reason of causes earlier mentioned should not be included," Davide added. Literal interpretation risks injustice In concurring with Panganiban and Davide, Puno said Article XI Section 3.6 of the 1987 Constitution—which states that "concurrence of two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate" are required for conviction—cannot be interpreted literally because it did not mention any number in the first place. "I respectfully submit however that it is inappropriate to give Article XI Section 3.6 a standalone literal reading. If we give this kind of reading to Article XI Section 3.6 , the threshold of 16 senators to convict will be fixed and immutable. However, if that is the intent, Article XI Section 3.6 should have simply stated that the number of votes to convict is 16, period," Puno said. "But Article XI Section 3.6 did not say so. Instead, the language used a fraction. It says two-thirds of all members of the Senate. By using two-thirds, the number of votes to convict will have to move depending on certain factors. A strict, standalone, literal interpretation of Article XI Section 3.6 may result in absurdities and may result in injustices which will defeat the purpose of the Constitution," Puno added. EXPLAINER: Who are the impeachment court's amici curiae? For these reasons, Puno said that there should be contextual and functional interpretation of the Constitution. He said the voting provision should not be interpreted in isolation, but in relation to other provisions of the Charter "in order to give life to its purpose." "This [contextual and functional approach] will give the Senators the right to consider whether Senators who are already dead, resigned or expelled should still be counted in determining two-thirds of all the members of the Senate. Also, this approach will enable the Senators to consider whether Senators who are legally incapacitated like a Senator charged with plunder, like Senators under preventive suspension should still be counted in determining the number of votes to convict that is two-thirds of all the members of the Senate," Puno added. Ultimately, Puno said that the provisions of the Constitution “should not be interpreted narrowly or pedantically for the prescriptions therein are not mathematical formulas.” May cast a vote For his part, Azcuna, expressed belief that the 16-vote threshold is immovable. "Whether or not a senator-judge who did not attend or substantially participate in the impeachment proceedings asked among others profound questions to and observed the demeanor of witnesses may nevertheless validly cast a vote on the final question in an impeachment trial," Azcuna said. Azcuna, however, said Senate can implement specific rules on this since this is an internal matter. "This is an internal matter for the Senate to decide, according to a rule it may adapt on this basis," Azcuna said. Azcuna said the wording of the concurrence requirement is "not a technicality or an accident in drafting." He expressed belief that it prevents the impeachment from becoming a "routine weapon of partisan competition." — VDV GMA News

output.title: Ex-CJ Panganiban asks: Can senators be impeachment judges 'in the shadows of absence?' | ABS-CBN News
output.description: Retired Chief Justice Artemio Panganiban offered a path for the Senate court to resolve the contentious question of what is the least number of votes to secure
output.text: Retired Supreme Court Chief Justices Artemio Panganiban appears at the Senate impeachment court on Sept. 16, 2026 as amicus curiae, or "a friend of the court" to provide legal guidance on the constitutional voting threshold required for conviction. Maria Tan, ABS-CBN News MANILA — Retired Chief Justice Artemio Panganiban on Wednesday offered a path for the Senate impeachment court to resolve the contentious question of what is the least number of votes to secure a conviction in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, saying senator-judges should be guided by truth and fairness. The Senate court has paused hearings for Duterte's trial to hear opinions from retired magistrates invited as amici curiae or "friends of the court" on the issue of conviction threshold. One of the amici curiae invited by the Senate, Panganiban said the impeachment court, called sui generis or "of its own kind," should interpret the 1987 Constitution to reflect the "common sense" of the people guided by two fundamental standards: truth and fairness. Senator-judges should themselves be present in the trial to see whether "witnesses are telling the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth" and that fairness means "we hear before we condemn, that all sides are given the opportunity to explain," he said. "In this connection, is it truthful and fair to allow senators to cast their votes despite being absent from the proceedings? Is it fair and truthful should the senators be allowed to vote, though they were there in hiding, abroad, legally detained, sick, hospitalized, or otherwise absent, and have not been able to access and examine the documents? Have not heard the testimonies, and have not observed the demeanor of the witnesses?" said Panganiban. "Is it truthful and fair to the parties, to our country, and to our people, to allow those abroad? ... Can such duty be performed in the shadows of absence? Nor from legal impediments?" Active participation and an independent evaluation of the evidence are "essential to discharge the Senate's and the senators' constitutional responsibility," he also said. Davide: No impeach vote for senators charged with plunder, whereabouts unknown The Senate court is confronted with the difficult task of resolving questions surrounding the conviction threshold following absences from several members of the 24-seat chamber. Sen. Ronald dela Rosa has been in hiding for being wanted by the International Criminal Court for his role in former President Rodrigo Duterte's brutal drug war. Sen. Jinggoy Estrada and Sen. Rodante Marcoleta, meanwhile, are detained over plunder cases. Participants in the impeachment trial had put forward differing views on how to interpret the constitutional provision guiding the Senate on the voting threshold to convict an impeached official. Article XI Section 3(6) of the 1987 Constitution states: "The Senate shall have the sole power to try and decide all cases of impeachment. When sitting for that purpose, the Senators shall be on oath or affirmation... No person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate." Some say the conviction threshold could be lowered because the constitution used the term "two-thirds" and that it is open to interpretation, but others argue that the number is fixed to 16 votes as the Senate is composed of 24 members. Panganiban also stressed that whatever the decision of the Senate court on Duterte's case is "final and unappealable" and the "only way" that the Supreme Court can step in to review its ruling is if the chamber "commits grave abuse of discretion." Prosecutors need to secure a guilty verdict on at least one article of impeachment to convict Duterte. WATCH:

output.title: Ex-Pres. Rodrigo Duterte, mananatiling nakadetine sa ICC, ayon sa pasya ng trial chamber
output.description: Nagkakaisa sa desisyon ang mga hukom ng Trial Chamber III ng International Criminal Court (ICC) na panatilihing nakadetine si dating Pangulong Rodrigo Duterte.
output.text: Nagkakaisa sa desisyon ang mga hukom ng Trial Chamber III ng International Criminal Court (ICC) na panatilihing nakadetine si dating Pangulong Rodrigo Duterte. Sa desisyong inilabas ilang sandali matapos ang ikatlong status conference, sinabi ng Chamber na may posibilidad na si Duterte na, “absconding and/or obstructing or endangering the investigation or the court proceedings.” “In respect of the latter considerations, owing to the Prosecution’s submission of the Witness and Evidence Lists, (thereby disclosing the identities of the witnesses and the contents of their expected testimony), this increases the Accused’s ability to interfere with witnesses, either directly or through his family or supporters in the Philippines,” nakasaad sa desisyon. Samantala, hindi pa napagpasyahan ng mga hukom ang usapin tungkol sa kalusugan ni Duterte kung kakayanin niyang humarap sa paglilitis. Ito ay matapos na humiling ang panig ng depensa ng “greater medical certainty,” habang kinukuwestiyon ang ulat ng mga sumuring grupo ng eksperto. Gayunman, sinabi ng Chamber na ang mga obserbasyon ng mga abogado ni Duterte ay hindi nagbibigay ng, “any information that constitutes new facts or a change in circumstances” na maaaring maging dahilan upang baguhin ang kaniyang pagkakadetine. Hiniling naman ng Office of the Prosecutor ng ICC sa Trial Chamber III na ipagpatuloy ang pagdetine kay Duterte, at sinabing kinakailangan ito upang hindi nito mapanghimasukan ang mga testigo. Sinabi ni Acting Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang na walang pagbabago sa kalagayan ni Duterte na magiging dahilan upang baguhin ng Trial Chamber III ang nauna nitong utos tungkol sa pagdetine sa dating pangulo. Sa pagdinig nitong Miyerkoles, muling nakita ng publiko si Duterte sa unang pagkakataon mula nang madetine siya sa ICC noong 2025, matapos siyang dumalo sa status conference kaugnay ng kaniyang kaso na crimes against humanity. “This is the first time that Mr. Duterte has been in this court. As far as the trial chamber is concerned, if he wishes to leave for any reason, he may do so,” saad ni Presiding Judge Joanna Korner. Nakatakdang magsimula ang paglilitis laban kay Duterte sa darating na November 30. Nahaharap siya sa mga kasong crimes against humanity kaugnay ng mga nangyaring patayan sa kaniyang war on drugs campaign noong nakaupo siyang pangulo ng bansa, at bilang alkalde ng Davao City. Inaresto si Duterte noong Marso 2025 sa Terminal 3 ng Ninoy Aquino International Airport at kasalukuyang nakakulong sa ICC Detention Centre sa Scheveningen sa The Hague, Netherlands. — Andy Peñafuerte III/FRJ GMA News

output.text: The House prosecution panel presents NBI Senior Agent John Mark Calilung, from the Cybercrime Investigation Unit, to testify on the Article IV charges of culpable violation of the Constitution, high crimes, and betrayal of public trust during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on July 7, 2026. Joseph B. Vidal, Senate Social Media Unit MANILA -- As the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte enters its second week, House prosecutor Representative Leila De Lima expects that the next witness from the National Bureau of Investigation will fortify the foundations laid by the prosecution's first witness, NBI senior agent John Mark Calilung. NBI Regional Director and senior agent, lawyer Jeremy Lotoc is expected to take the witness stand on Monday, July 13 as the trial continues to tackle the fourth Article of Impeachment -- the alleged assassination plot arranged by Duterte against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and the president's cousin, former House Speaker Martin Romualdez. Inside the session hall: The first 3 days of VP Duterte's impeachment trial "Dadagdagan 'yung testimonya ni Senior Agent Mark Calilung. Papalakasin syempre kasi pundasyon lang 'yun. So brick by brick, we're going to make it stronger. The evidence against VP Sara, against the respondent is for Article 4. So mostly, mainly, testimonial evidence," she said in a news forum Saturday, July 11. Lotoc is the NBI investigator who led the probe into Duterte's alleged threat, according to De Lima. "He will both be corroborating as well as adding certain aspects to the testimony of Agent Calilung. Lalo na doon sa pinaka-imbestigasyon mismo at ano ang resulta, ano 'yung basehan nung kanilang konklusyon kung bakit rinifer nila o finorward nila sa DOJ," she added. Lotoc is expected to lay down the circumstances, the context and the "seriousness" of the vice president's alleged kill plot given the results of the bureau's investigation. "We cannot at this point disclose kung ano 'yung direction or focus ng investigation especially that of course she will be presented as a hostile witness," the lawmaker-prosecutor noted. "Tandaan din po natin na ang pag-a-assess po ng prosecution kung sino at ano ang ebidensya ay base 'yan, that would depend on the outcome of the testimony of the preceding witness," she added. De Lima noted that the identification of next witnesses to take the stand would depend on the outcome of Lotoc's testimony. "So, isusunod ba kaagad si Atty. Zuleika o meron ho bang dapat na ipresenta after Atty. Lotoc. It depends now on the outcome of the testimony of Atty. Lotoc," she said. "Kasi sila mismo, yung kabila, napansin niyo po, na actually, nagpakita rin po sila ng certain portions of the video. So admission po 'yun. Nagpapakita na wala silang kinikwestiyon sa pagdating sa issue ng authenticity," she said. 'DOUBLE MEANING?' Meanwhile, De Lima also weighed in on the remark of OVP Chief of Staff Zuleika Lopez during her Senate visit on July 9 where the latter told reporters, "Prepare for Typhoon Inday." "Merong double meaning 'yang ganyang salita," De Lima asserted. "Inday" is both the name of a typhoon and the nickname of Duterte. "So literally, tama 'yun, prepare for Typhoon Inday. Pero pwede rin natin ma-interpret in another manner, it has to do with the impeachment. Meron na naman bang kababalaghang pinaplano 'yung kabila, 'yung kampo ni VP Sara para madiskarel, maka-delay dito sa impeachment trial?" she said. "So double meaning po yun, we just hope that she's just referring to the first meaning, the first literal meaning of that statement," De Lima stated. output.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial, Week 11: Trial moves from wealth records to vote math
output.description: The impeachment trial took an unexpected turn on Day 26, when the Senate heard four retired Supreme Court justices on a separate but potentially crucial question: whether the two-thirds vote required to convict Duterte should always mean 16 votes in the 24-member Senate.
output.text: Tita C. Valderama is an editor and trustee of VERA Files. She has been a journalist for more than 30 years. The House prosecution panel this week began presenting witnesses and records to build its case of alleged unexplained wealth against Vice President Sara Duterte, putting her financial declarations and accountability as a public official under scrutiny for the first time in the impeachment trial. The prosecution’s presentation of Article II, which covers allegations of unexplained wealth, SALN discrepancies and business interests, began with retired Sandiganbayan Presiding Justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang on Day 24, and continued with Ombudsman records officer Karen Batu on Day 25. Cabotaje-Tang laid out the legal standards for determining unexplained wealth and the obligations of public officials, while Batu authenticated Duterte’s Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth from 2007 to 2025, giving the Senate impeachment court a nearly two-decade record of her declared wealth. The prosecution’s evidence did not by itself establish wrongdoing. But it marked a shift in the trial from the presentation of evidence on other impeachment allegations to a closer examination of Duterte’s wealth, SALNs and financial interests. The week then took an unexpected turn on Day 26, when the Senate heard four retired Supreme Court justices on a separate but potentially crucial question: whether the two-thirds vote required to convict Duterte should always mean 16 votes in the 24-member Senate. The four amici curiae – retired chief justices Hilario Davie Jr., Artemio Panganiban and Reynato Pun0, and associate justice Adolfo Azuna – offered differing views on how “two-thirds of all the members of the Senate” should be interpreted when some senators are unable to participate in the trial, setting up another major constitutional dispute. Cabotaje-Tang, the prosecution’s first witness for Article II, did not testify that Duterte had unexplained wealth. She said she had no personal knowledge of Duterte’s properties, stocks or bonds, or of the accuracy of her SALNs. Instead, the retired justice explained the legal framework that the prosecution said would guide the court in assessing the financial records it planned to present. She testified that wealth acquired during a public official’s incumbency could be considered questionable when it was grossly disproportionate to the official’s salary, lawful income and earnings from legitimately acquired property. She also discussed the requirement for public officials to disclose their assets through their SALNs, including cash on hand and cash in bank. She said these should be separately declared and should not simply be lumped under other personal property. But Cabotaje-Tang cautioned that a single failure to declare an asset does not automatically establish intentional concealment. Repeated omissions, however, could carry greater weight and, when an asset was omitted over several years, could be a “badge” of attempted concealment. She also explained the constitutional restrictions on the president and vice president engaging directly or indirectly in business while in office. The Constitution bars the president and vice president from practicing a profession, participating in business or having financial interests in government contracts, franchises or special privileges during their tenure. The former Sandiganbayan chief also testified that assets could be concealed through dummies, nominees or proxies, including property placed in another person’s name. The defense sought to cast doubt on her testimony during cross-examination, asking whether she was “anti-Duterte” or “ Kakampink ,” whether she had been disappointed after failing to get an appointment to the Supreme Court and whether she was seeking an ambassadorship. Cabotaje-Tang denied having any political agenda. “I’ve never been political in my life. I’ve always been apolitical,” she said. Asked if she had been promised anything in exchange for her testimony, she replied: “I will never testify if I ever was offered anything material or otherwise… My testimony is not for sale, sir.” She said she was retired and wanted to enjoy her retirement. SALNs put Duterte’s wealth on record On Day 25, the prosecution moved from legal principles to Duterte’s actual SALNs. Lawyer Karen Batu, officer in charge of the Ombudsman’s Central Records Division, authenticated Duterte’s SALNs covering 2007 to 2025. The records showed that Duterte declared a net worth of P7.25 million in 2007, when she began her political career as Davao City vice mayor. Her declared net worth rose to P18.49 million in 2008 and reached P98.66 million in 2025. “After one year lang sa public office, doble na ang itinaas ng net worth, based on records only,” private prosecutor James Bryan Ibrahim Alih noted. The 2008 figure was actually 2.55 times her 2007 net worth, while the 2025 figure was about 13.6 times her 2007 net worth. The figures, however, are declarations on SALNs and do not by themselves establish that any wealth was unlawfully acquired. The prosecution also focused on Duterte’s declarations of business and financial interests. Batu testified that Duterte declared no shares in 2007, then listed “stocks equity paid” in 2008. In subsequent years, she listed various business or financial interests, but the SALNs did not consistently state the number or value of shares. The issue prompted questions from the senator-judges on whether the absence of acquisition costs could affect the declared value of the interests. Batu repeatedly stressed that her office was only the custodian of the SALNs. It did not verify whether the information supplied by public officials was complete or accurate. That limitation became important as the defense challenged the prosecution’s use of SALNs filed before Duterte became vice president. Presiding Officer Francis Escudero allowed the older SALNs to be presented, saying the records could establish a baseline for determining changes in Duterte’s wealth during her impeachable term. Batu also testified that Duterte declared cash on hand and in bank accounts in earlier years, including P2 million in 2007 and 2008, and increasing amounts in succeeding years. But from 2019 through 2025, Duterte’s SALNs contained no declared cash on hand or in bank. The prosecution said the long record of SALNs would allow the court to compare Duterte’s declared wealth over time with other financial records that it plans to present. That paper trail is expected to include bank, corporate and other financial documents obtained through subpoenas. The prosecution still has to connect those records to Duterte’s lawful income, declared assets and business interests to establish its allegations. The vote question takes center stage Then came Day 26, when the impeachment court temporarily shifted from Duterte’s wealth to the constitutional mechanics of the trial itself. The four retired Supreme Court justices appeared as amici curiae, or friends of the court, to address whether 16 votes should remain the fixed requirement for conviction. Their intervention was deemed important after Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo suggested on Sept. 8 that the court to revisit Escudero’s July 6 ruling that 16 votes would be needed to convict an impeachable official. “When we refer to all members, who exactly are we counting?” Tulfo had asked. Article XI, Section 3(6) of the 1987 Constitution provides that an impeached official cannot be convicted “without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the members of the Senate.” The dispute centers on whether “all members” should mean all 24 senators regardless of their ability to participate, or only those legally able to take part in the impeachment proceedings and final vote. Four senators are currently unable to attend the trial: Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, who is in hiding amid an International Criminal Court arrest warrant; Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta, who are facing nonbailable plunder charges before the Sandiganbayan; and Loren Legarda, who is reportedly in France on an extended medical leave since Aug. 3. Estrada, Marcoleta and Dela Rosa have not attended a single impeachment trial. Their absence prompts the question of whether the 16-vote requirement should remain despite the reduced number of participating senator-judges. Retired chief justices Hilario Davide Jr., Artemio Panganiban and Reynato Puno said the number could change depending on which senators are legally capable of participating in the proceedings. Retired Associate Justice Adolfo Azcuna took the opposite position. Davide, in a memorandum submitted to the court, said the phrase “all the members of the Senate” should refer to senators who are qualified to exercise their constitutional functions. “Those who are detained, abroad, suspended or whose whereabouts are unknown cannot be included, or must be excluded, from the phrase ‘all the Members of the Senate’,” he said. Davide added that senators who had resigned, been expelled, become incapacitated, gone into hiding, been outside Philippine jurisdiction or were legally restrained from performing their duties should also be excluded from the computation. “Clearly then, the basis of computing the two-thirds must be the number of senators who are qualified to vote, not the 24 in the present Senate,” Davide said. Panganiban similarly said the constitutional phrase should not be treated as a mathematical formula detached from the circumstances of the case. “Reality, sometimes, Your Honors, changes the denominator in mathematics,” he told the court. He questioned whether a senator who was detained, hospitalized, abroad or otherwise unable to participate meaningfully in the proceedings should nevertheless be counted in determining the votes needed for conviction. “Is it truthful and fair to the parties, to our country, and to our people, to allow those abroad, those looking at the pyramids along the Nile, or shopping in the fashion houses of Paris, or riding the romantic gondolas of Venice, or deliberately hiding in the dark corners of the world while everyone here, everyone here in this hall is sweating it out, listening to sometimes irrelevant and loquacious lawyers, or to humble an ancient amicus curiae like me?” he asked. “Meaningful adjudication requires active participation in the search for truth and fairness,” Panganiban said. Puno also rejected the idea that the Constitution necessarily fixed the number at 16. He pointed out that the Constitution says “two-thirds of all the members of the Senate,” rather than simply specifying 16 votes. For him, the phrase allows the court to consider circumstances that affect a senator’s ability to perform the functions of a senator-judge. Azcuna disagreed. “All means all,” he said, arguing that all 24 sitting senators should remain part of the denominator as long as they remain members of the Senate. He warned that allowing the threshold to change according to attendance could make the required vote variable. “A threshold must be fixed, not variable. It must be determinable from the start,” he said. The four justices also differed on whether senators who had missed portions of the trial could still vote. Panganiban stressed the importance of active participation and independent assessment of the evidence. Puno and Azcuna, however, said a senator could evaluate the record even without personally hearing every witness. Davide said a senator who never attended or performed any duties in the trial could be treated differently, although merely failing to question witnesses would not necessarily make a senator a nonparticipant. All four agreed that the 1967 Supreme Court decision in Avelino v. Cuenco, which dealt with Senate quorum, did not directly resolve the impeachment vote question. The justices differed only on how useful the ruling might be by analogy. The contrast in the four positions underscored the unusual nature of the issue. The disagreement was not over whether the Constitution requires two-thirds, but over what “all the members” means when some senators cannot take part. The court’s current ruling remains that 16 votes are needed to convict. The issue will be argued further on Sept. 23 when the defense and prosecution will have their oral arguments, before the impeachment court decides whether to retain or revisit that ruling. output.title: Prosecution still weighing possibility of putting Madriaga on witness stand—Ridon | ABS-CBN News
output.description: The House prosecution panel is still weighing whether to put Ramil Madriaga on the witness stand, even as it assesses whether the testimony of former Office of
output.text: Former Special Disbursing Officer (SDO) of the Office of the Vice President (OVP) Gina Acosta takes her oath as a hostile witness for the prosecution during the 16th day of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte at the Senate in Pasay City on Monday, August 17, 2026. Maria Tan, ABS-CBN News MANILA – The House prosecution panel is still weighing whether to put Ramil Madriaga on the witness stand, even as it assesses whether the testimony of former Office of the Vice President special disbursing officer Gina Acosta can already establish key parts of its case against Vice President Sara Duterte. Prosecution member Rep. Teddy Ridon said the panel has yet to make a final decision on Madriaga, whose credibility has been repeatedly challenged by the defense. Who is Ramil Madriaga? “We've still yet to make a determination kung isasalang ba siya o hindi, in the similar manner na we’ll still decide if Mr. Lachica o Mr. Nolasco will still be presented. Wala namang mababawas sa defense para isalang si Mr. Mardriaga, kasama rin siya sa mga common witnesses namin,” Ridon said on DZMM TeleRadyo, Saturday morning. The issue came after defense lawyer Paolo Panelo described Madriaga’s possible appearance as “the prosecution’s funeral,” saying the defense would tear him apart during cross-examination. Duterte has also filed a second perjury complaint against Madriaga, accusing him of making false statements in a supplemental affidavit. Sara Duterte’s camp to seek consolidation of perjury complaints vs Ramil Madriaga But Ridon questioned why Panelo was commenting on the prosecution’s witness strategy. “Lagi kong sinasabi, hindi naman siya kasama sa defense panel. Bakit siya nagsasalita tungkol doon sa impeachment presentation of evidence?” Ridon said. He added that Madriaga is also considered a common witness. “Wala namang mababawas sa defense para isalang si Mr. Madriaga,” Ridon said. “Kung tingin talaga ni Atty. Panelo na makatutulong 'yung sinasabi niya sa defense panel, edi sabihin niya sa defense panel. Huwag niya sabihin sa prosecution.” The prosecution had previously sought Madriaga’s testimony during the House proceedings, where he made allegations involving Duterte. HOW STRONG IS ACOSTA'S TESTIMONY? Ridon said the prosecution views Acosta's testimony potentially sufficient to establish the alleged misuse of confidential funds, particularly her claim that Duterte ordered the release of P125 million to then-OVP security officer Col. Raymund Lachica. “Kung ‘yung pagpapatunay sa confidential misuse ay ‘yung fact pa lang na talagang tinuro ni Ms. Acosta si Vice President Sara Duterte, na inutos ‘yung P125 million confidential funds ni Mr. Lachica, ‘yon pa lang sufficient proof na ‘yon nong misuse,” he said. “‘Yan mismo ‘yung binabanggit ng notice of disallowance for 2023 na nagbigay po ng pera sa mga non-OVP personnel like Mr. Lachica,” he added. Ridon said Acosta’s testimony in the impeachment trial has been consistent with her previous statements before the House of Representatives during the 19th Congress. “Ang totoo, it really confirmed doon sa House proceedings noong 19th Congress na meroon talagang consistency ang statement ni Ms. Acosta, and more importantly, ‘yung kaniyang estado bilang hostile witness na meron talagang similar interest as Vice President,” Ridon said. Acosta, a former special disbursing officer of the Office of the Vice President, had previously testified during the House inquiry that after encashing the OVP’s confidential funds, she turned over the cash to then-Vice Presidential Security and Protection Group head Col. Raymund Dante Lachica, a military officer, allegedly upon the instruction of Vice President Duterte. Prosecution: Acosta testimony ‘major’ as she points to Sara Duterte Meanwhile, former Department of Education special disbursing officer Edward Fajarda had also testified during the House proceedings that he turned over the DepEd confidential funds he withdrew to Col. Dennis Nolasco, then a security officer of the agency, allegedly upon Duterte’s instruction. Acosta was declared a hostile witness by the Senate impeachment court on Aug. 17 after prosecutors sought to question her using leading questions. ‘NOT YET FINISHED’ Ridon said Acosta’s testimony is not yet finished. “There are still many questions doon sa direct ni Atty. Ligutan na hindi pa po natanong,” he said. The prosecution expects the next hearing to include extensive cross-examination by the defense, followed by questions from the senator-judges. “We’re expecting an entire session of cross,” Ridon said, adding that Acosta could finish her testimony by Tuesday or Wednesday. After Acosta, the prosecution expects to call Fajarda, who is expected to testify about the alleged transfer of confidential funds from the Department of Education to personnel who were not organic DepEd employees. Ridon said the prosecution will then determine whether other witnesses, including Lachica and Nolasco, are still necessary. WRAP: Confidential funds released to OVP security chief as Duterte ordered — Acosta ACCELERATE IMPEACHMENT TRIAL The questions surrounding Acosta and Madriaga come as the prosecution pushes to accelerate the impeachment trial. Ridon said the prosecution supports proposals to add hearing days and extend proceedings into the afternoon and evening. The panel hopes to finish presenting its evidence by the end of September, in line with the broader target of completing the trial proceedings by November and reaching a decision by December. But Ridon stressed that the prosecution does not want to sacrifice the quality of its evidence simply to meet a deadline. “Wala naman kaming interes na madaliin for the sake of madaliin,” he said. He rejected the characterization of the trial as a battle of competing narratives. “This is not a battle of narrative, this is a battle of evidence,” Ridon said. The House-approved impeachment case contains four articles involving allegations including the misuse and irregular liquidation of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery, and alleged threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. Ridon said the prosecution has yet to make a final decision on whether to drop Article 3, with bribery and unexplained wealth still in its planned sequence. For now, the prosecution’s immediate focus, Ridon said, remains on the confidential-funds allegations and on whether Acosta’s testimony can withstand the scrutiny of the defense, or whether additional witnesses such as Madriaga will be needed to strengthen the case. output.title: Provisional list of witnesses vs Duterte submitted
output.description: The Office of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court has submitted a provisional list of witnesses that it intends to present in the case against former president Rodrigo Duterte.
output.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court (ICC) has submitted a provisional list of witnesses that it intends to present in the case against former president Rodrigo Duterte. The submission of the list was confirmed in a filing dated June 29 and made public yesterday. The names of the potential witnesses, however, remained confidential. “The prosecution has provided the pseudonym for each witness. The prosecution notes that the number of witnesses is likely to increase from the Provisional List of Witnesses in light of the prosecution’s ongoing investigations,” read the filing signed by ICC deputy prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang. Niang told the trial judges that the prosecution will provide additional details, including the summary of the witnesses’ testimony, when it submits the final list on Aug. 31. The trial of the 81-year-old Duterte, who is facing charges of crimes against humanity, is expected to start on Nov. 30. Niang earlier said the prosecution may rely on evidence from 60 to 70 witnesses during the trial, further investigations and addition of potential witnesses. These include 31 insider witnesses, 17 crime-based witnesses and 12 others “who are relevant to explain the background and the contextual elements of the crimes charged.” The prosecutor intends to call 25 to 30 witnesses to provide viva voce or verbal testimony during the trial. The rest of the witnesses will be presented under ICC’s Rule 68, which allows “the introduction of previously recorded audio or video testimony of a witness, or the transcript or other documented evidence of such testimony.” “The prosecution intends to call as many of its witnesses as possible to testify in person at the seat of the Court,” Niang said in his May 15 filing. “However, the prosecution anticipates that some witnesses may need to testify via audio/video link where the witness is unable to travel to the seat of the Court,” he added. The prosecution estimated that its direct examination of the witnesses could take 175 to 200 hours. The ICC Trial Chamber III earlier reminded both parties to ensure that the presentation of evidence “must take place in the shortest and clearest way” and that unnecessary and lengthy legal arguments should be avoided. output.title: Drug war victims’ lawyers maintain Duterte is fit to stand trial based on expert panel conclusions | ABS-CBN News
output.description: The legal representatives for victims in the International Criminal Court proceedings involving former president Rodrigo Duterte have maintained that the legal
output.text: Former President Rodrigo Duterte appears before the International Criminal Court during its third status conference at the ICC headquarters in The Hague on September 16, 2026. ICC screengrab MANILA — The legal representatives for victims in the International Criminal Court proceedings involving former president Rodrigo Roa Duterte have maintained that the legal criteria for an accused person’s fitness to stand trial are fully satisfied, pointing to unanimous findings from a panel of medical experts. “The CLRV (Common Legal Representatives of the Victims) submit that the applicable legal criteria governing an accused’s fitness to stand trial are satisfied under the established jurisprudence of the Court… In light of these clear and consistent scientific conclusions, the CLRV submit that the legal criteria governing fitness to stand trial under the established jurisprudence of the Court are fully satisfied in the present case,” they said. In a public redacted version of their observations filed on September 17, 2026, the CLRV comprising Gilbert Andres, Joel Butuyan, and Paolina Massidda, concluded that the court “is entitled to find that Mr Duterte is fit to stand trial.” Rodrigo Duterte makes first in-person appearance at ICC The filing centers on the evaluation of joint and individual reports submitted by a multidisciplinary panel of experts on August 21, 2026. According to the CLRV, the experts unanimously concluded that despite certain conditions noted in the report, Duterte possesses the capacity required to stand trial. The CLRV noted that the panel found “no new evidence.” Drug war victims’ families express mixed emotions over Duterte’s ICC appearance The procedural history outlined in the submission shows that the defense previously requested an indefinite adjournment of the proceedings in August 2025. Following an initial medical examination, the Pre-Trial Chamber found Duterte fit to participate in pre-trial proceedings in January 2026 and confirmed the charges against him in April 2026, after which the case was referred to the Chamber. ICC says Duterte 'shall continue to be detained' A second medical examination was subsequently ordered on June 12, 2026, to determine whether the accused's medical condition had changed. The resulting August reports prompted the recent round of observations regarding the practical measures needed to facilitate participation. Duterte in ICC: Prosecution, Defense debate on evidence at 3rd status conference Citing established court jurisprudence, including principles referenced in the case, the CLRV reaffirmed that “the ability of an accused, viewed overall and in a reasonable manner, to understand and participate in the proceedings and to instruct counsel is central to a finding that they are fit to stand trial.” “In light of these clear and consistent scientific conclusions, the CLRV submit that the legal criteria governing fitness to stand trial under the established jurisprudence of the Court are fully satisfied in the present case,” they said. While acknowledging that the experts recommended specific measures to facilitate attendance and participation, the CLRV stated they "do not oppose the adoption of reasonable accommodations, provided that such measures do not prejudice the rights of other participants or the orderly conduct of the proceedings." The filing concludes with a direct request for the Chamber to formally determine that Duterte is fit to stand trial.

output.title: ICC weighs prosecutor’s demand to keep Duterte detained pending fitness ruling | ABS-CBN News
output.description: Trial chambers at the International Criminal Court weigh opposing arguments over whether former Philippine President Rodrigo Roa Duterte should remain behind ba
output.text: Rights advocates from Karapatan holds a press conference at the Ambai Modern Tambayan restaurant in Quezon City on September 9, 2025 on the ICC's postponement of the confirmation of charges of Rodrigo Duterte.The victims and their families, fear that any postponement in the proceedings gives the Dutertes the opportunity to harass, endanger or even eliminate the prosecution witnesses. Jonathan Cellona, ABS-CBN News/File MANILA — Trial chambers at the International Criminal Court weigh opposing arguments over whether former Philippine President Rodrigo Roa Duterte should remain behind bars as legal proceedings against him advance. The Office of the Prosecutor has urged the court to keep Duterte in custody, arguing that recent developments in the case have heightened the risks of him fleeing or tampering with witnesses. Meanwhile, the legal team representing the former president has opted not to file substantive arguments on his detention at this stage, pointing instead to a pending medical evaluation regarding his fitness to stand trial. “The Defense informed the Chamber, parties and participants on 4 September 2024 that 'it does not intend to submit observations at this time', but that it anticipated coming back as required after the question of the accused’s fitness to stand trial had been settled… The Defense raised the issue of Mr Duterte’s fitness on 25 May 2026, and requested that Mr Duterte undergo a medical examination to assess his fitness to stand trial,” as explained under submissions of Mr. Duterte’s defence team. Under International Criminal Court rules, Trial Chamber III is required to periodically review the detention of an accused person within a 120-day timeframe, prompting the current round of submissions filed on September 14, 2026. “The Trial Chamber acknowledged the Defense’s submission that it did not intend to submit observations on Mr Duterte’s detention at this time, but 'bearing in mind the obligation of the Chamber to rule on this matter by the upcoming 120-day time limit pursuant to Rule 118(2) of the Rules' noted that 'the Defense may address this issue in writing no later than 14 September 2026.'” PROSECUTION CITES HEIGHTENED RISKS In its observations submitted to the court, the prosecution maintained that the legal conditions requiring Duterte's detention under the Rome Statute remain fully met. Acting Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang argued that circumstances have not changed in a way that warrants release; rather, developments have amplified the risks associated with the accused. “To the contrary, there have been changes in circumstances that have increased the risk Mr Duterte presents under articles 58(1)(b)(i) and (ii) of the Statute,” as explained in the document by the office of the prosecutor. The prosecution pointed to two main factors increasing the risk of flight under Article 58(1)(b)(i) of the statute. First, "recent advancements in this case have increased the prospect of Mr Duterte facing trial," noting that a definitive trial date has now been set. Second, prosecutors have expanded the scope of the case, having "added eight additional incidents to Mr Duterte's charges since the date of the Decision." According to the prosecution, the expanding "number of incidents and victims, and therefore the prospect of a lengthy prison sentence, have increased, which militates in favor of Mr Duterte's continued detention." Furthermore, prosecutors argued that the risk of witness interference has grown. On August 31, 2026, the prosecution provided its official List of Witnesses and related evidence to the defense. This disclosure supplies the defense with names, expected testimonies, and other sensitive details. “The List of Witnesses provides Mr Duterte with the names of the Prosecution's witnesses, 10 as well as their expected testimony, and [REDACTED]." Emphasizing that the evaluation of witness risks "revolves around the possibility, not the inevitability, of a future occurrence," the prosecution asserted that "Mr Duterte's history shows that he is able and has the means, either directly or through his associates, to interfere with" the proceedings. Consequently, prosecutors requested that the chamber order his continued detention. DEFENSE AWAITS FITNESS DETERMINATION The defense response, led by counsel Peter Haynes, KC, took a different procedural track. Following an order from the Trial Chamber, the defense initially informed the court that "it does not intend to submit observations at this time," anticipating that it would return to the matter once a critical preliminary issue is resolved. “It anticipated coming back as required after the question of the accused’s fitness to stand trial had been settled,” explained under the defense’s submissions. Although the chamber subsequently issued a reminder noting the mandatory 120-day review deadline and offering a September 14 deadline for written inputs, the defense maintained its position. The core of the defense's current stance centers on health and competency. Back on May 25, 2026, the defense raised the issue of Duterte’s medical fitness and requested an examination to determine whether he is capable of standing trial. While parties have submitted their positions based on medical expert findings, a formal ruling from the Trial Chamber is still pending. The defense argued that the two matters are inherently connected, noting that "should Mr Duterte be found unfit to stand trial and the proceedings consequently adjourned, this would be relevant to the assessment of whether there has been a material change in circumstances." Rather than engaging with the detention review immediately, the defense stated it "anticipates exercising its right under Rule 118(2) to seek a review of the detention regime once the Trial Chamber has determined Mr Duterte’s fitness to stand trial, if the circumstances merit it." With both filings now before The Hague, Trial Chamber III faces the task of weighing the prosecution's observations on the former Philippine President’s detention against the defense's pending fitness evaluations as the legal process moves forward. output.title: ICC denies Duterte appeal vs fitness to stand trial ruling
output.description: The International Criminal Court on Friday denied the request of the camp of former President Rodrigo Duterte to challenge its ruling deeming him fit to face prosecution for crimes against humanity.
output.text: The International Criminal Court on Friday denied the request of the camp of former President Rodrigo Duterte to challenge its ruling deeming him fit to face prosecution for crimes against humanity. In its request , the defense argued the Pre-Trial Chamber I "erred in fact and in law" by ignoring relevant clinical evidence on Duterte’s lack of fitness to stand trial and rejecting the request to hold a hearing on the matter. The defense also accused the chamber of failing to articulate coherently its decision to proceed with the confirmation proceedings, limiting its assessment of the former president's fitness to the pre-trial phase, and failing to consider the impact of its finding on Duterte’s ability to stand trial. However, the three-person chamber said the panel of experts took into consideration the reports provided by the defense when assessing Duterte's health condition. It also said the defense's arguments in relation to Duterte's "memory impairment" were addressed in its January 26 ruling. "[I]t is clear that the Chamber’s reason not to rely on the defense’s medical reports was to ensure that only information emanating from impartial and neutral sources was taken into consideration in order to ultimately ensure the fairness of the proceedings," the chamber said. The chamber emphasized that the January 26 decision "does not prejudge Mr. Duterte’s fitness to stand trial and that it does not preclude any competent chamber of the Court [from revisiting] the issue should the need arise." "As argued by the defense and properly noted by the prosecution, Mr. Duterte’s fitness to stand trial is an issue that is likely to be revisited at trial, should all or some of the charges be confirmed," it said. In another development, the Court authorized 500 individuals to participate in the proceedings as "victims." It added that the Common Legal Representative for Victims, appointed to represent "any admitted victims in the present case," shall also represent these individuals. Duterte has been detained at the ICC in The Hague since March 12, 2025, while awaiting trial in connection with the alleged abuses in his war on drugs when he was Davao City mayor and president. The confirmation of charges hearing will begin on February 23 and will run until February 27. — VBL GMA Integrated News

It will also discuss the sitting schedule of the trial from November 30 until the Spring Recess in 2027. Aside from this, the Chamber will discuss the Registry’s proposal to have blocks of hearings with breaks and sitting hours in light of the experts’ recommendations. output.description: THE HAGUE, Netherlands - Former Philippines president Rodrigo Duterte is expected to arrive in the Netherlands on Wednesday to face a crime against humanity cha
output.text: THE HAGUE, Netherlands - Former Philippines president Rodrigo Duterte is expected to arrive in the Netherlands on Wednesday to face a crime against humanity charge stemming from his crackdown on drugs. Rodrigo Duterte and ICC: From years-long probe to 'unexpected' arrest After landing, he will be taken to the International Criminal Court's detention unit, where he will be readied for an initial appearance before the court's judges. War on Drugs, The Unheard Voices | ABS-CBN News Here is what he can expect: - The prison - Located in The Hague's seaside suburb of Scheveningen, the ICC's detention unit forms part of a Dutch prison and currently holds five other ICC prisoners being tried before the court. It is also the prison that used to detain those wanted by the nearby International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) including the likes of Slobodan Milosevic, Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic. "In fulfilling its mandate, the ICC Registrar endeavors to ensure the mental, physical and spiritual welfare of the detained persons within an efficient system of detention, with consideration to their cultural diversity and their development as individuals," the ICC says on its website. Prisoners all have individual cells equipped with computers, but no access to the internet, to allow them to work on their cases. The cells also have a bed, desk, shelves, a cupboard, toilet, hand basin, television and an intercom to speak to guards when the cell is locked. They may also use an outdoor exercise area and take part in sports and recreation activities. Three meals a day are served, but there is also a communal kitchen where detainees can cook with groceries provided from a shopping list "in order for them to adjust the meals provided to them, according to their taste and cultural requirements". Detainees may receive family or conjugal visits "several times a year" and if they are declared destitute, the court foots the bill for the visits "to the extent possible". - Initial appearance - ICC rules say all detainees "shall appear before the Pre-Trial Chamber, in the presence of the prosecutor, promptly upon arrival at the court". This hearing aims to verify a suspect's identity and to inform the arrested person of the crimes he or she is accused of. Prisoners are informed of their rights under the ICC's founding treaty, the Rome Statute, including the right to apply for interim release. Pre-trial judges will then set a date on which it will hold a confirmation of charges hearing. - Confirmation of charges - The Rome Statute says that within a reasonable amount of time after a person's surrender or detention, the Pre-Trial Chamber shall hold a hearing to "confirm the charges on which the prosecutor intends to seek trial". At that hearing, the prosecutor must convince judges that substantial grounds exist "to believe that the person committed the crime(s) charged" and that enough evidence had been gathered to hold a trial. The ICC's judges may at the end of the hearing either confirm the charges and send the accused to a trial chamber, or say more evidence is needed from the prosecutor, modify the charges, or drop the charges altogether. Once the charges have been confirmed, the court's presidency puts together a trial chamber to prepare and then conduct a trial. jhe/ric/phz © Agence France-Presse

output.title: Dispatch from the ICC grounds: A waving Duterte, tears of joy, delaying tactics
output.description: Just after the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III adjourned the third status conference for Rodrigo Duterte’s upcoming trial, the former president looked out and waved at viewers in the public gallery.
output.text: THE HAGUE Netherlands — Just after the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III adjourned the third status conference for Rodrigo Duterte’s upcoming trial, the former president looked out and waved at viewers in the public gallery. The gesture lasted only a few seconds as the gallery curtain closed, leaving several Duterte supporters tearing up. Unlike previous hearings in Duterte’s ICC case, only a few supporters attended today’s status conference, as they did not expect the former president to appear today. The other viewers were students touring the ICC, a handful of journalists, and other local visitors. “Looking good” The conference started promptly at 10:30 AM local time (4:30 PM Manila), with the gallery curtain slowly opening up. From our position in the media seats, Duterte was on the far end of the defense side. My journalist colleagues and I had been anticipating his appearance since there was no publicized request from his counsel, Peter Haynes, to waive his attendance before the court. As the judges entered the courtroom, Duterte was seated with his right hand on his chin – a posture reminiscent of one of his presidential portraits. Before the prosecution began their presentation, the journalists had a good five minutes spent observing the former president – who as the photos of the day show sports long hair and dons a black jacket and white inner shirt – before leaving the gallery to break the news. For some journalists, he was “looking good”, far from a mental image of an emaciated Duterte that his relatives had described some months back. A photojournalist, whom I briefly spoke with as I left the gallery, described Duterte as “looking happy” when she saw him entering the courtroom. She said the former president “invited” them to go to “our beautiful country of the Philippines.” “Tears of joy” When we returned to the gallery, I saw some smiling supporters locking their gaze on the former president, while others clasped their hands, as if praying. Janet Suliman, a long-time Duterte supporter, said she cried “tears of joy” when she saw Duterte – his first public appearance before the Court since March 14, 2025. She and other supporters told me they had expected him to appear in a wheelchair or in a visibly worse condition. “He’s a fighter,” Suliman said. “He looked confident. We believe he knows that he didn’t do anything wrong.” She added that they would continue to stand by Duterte “until the end” and that “justice would prevail.” I told Suliman that the relatives of drug war victims also want that justice as well. However, she said that some killed during the drug war “fought back” against the police. Other supporters, Cecil van Hameren, Alma Knoester, Jennifer Carcueba and Alvin Sarzate, questioned the volume of evidence the prosecution presented after Duterte’s defense said its evidence list had grown to nearly 20,000 items. They described the number as “unbelievable” and questioned how prosecutors could have gathered and prepared such a large amount of material. “Magician,” one supporter said, referring to the prosecution. Others dismissed the evidence as “made up” and “nonsense.” The prosecution has maintained that its evidence supports the charges against Duterte, while his defense team has raised separate concerns about the volume and organization of the material disclosed in the case. Delaying tactic The Duterte Panagutin Network (DPN) and other critics of the former president likewise anticipated his first appearance in court – but they rejected claims from his lawyers about his health and fitness to stand trial. Although none of the DPN members watched the conference in the gallery, they told me during their protest outside the ICC grounds that they would stay tuned, considering Duterte’s appearance before the court was already a “big win” for the relatives of drug war victims who yearn to hold him accountable. Fiona Magallanes of Bayan Netherlands and convenor of Panagutin Network Netherlands wrote in a statement that Duterte’s health arguments were his camp’s “delaying tactic”. She said the group hopes to see him appear again when his trial starts, which has been scheduled on November 30. "Duterte's appearance in court today proves he has been feigning sick all this time. It was all a delaying tactic, delaying justice and delaying healing for the victims’ families,” she said. Magallanes also said Duterte “looks well,” which she claimed was “exposing the myth that his camp has continuously pushed of a sickly old man supposedly ‘unfit to stand trial.’” Duterte’s lawyers have argued before the ICC that he suffers from cognitive impairment affecting his memory and ability to participate meaningfully in the proceedings. The Trial Chamber has yet to rule on his fitness to stand trial. Planned demonstrations The next status conference, based on the ICC court calendar, is scheduled for October 13. Duterte’s supporters told me they are gearing up for protests leading up to the November 30 trial. The Netherlands-based Duterte Panagutin Network, meanwhile, has already scheduled demonstrations on the first day of the trial. — BAP GMA News

output.title: Kitty Duterte stands by father Rodrigo Duterte at ICC appearance
output.description: Veronica “Kitty” Duterte on Thursday expressed her support for her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte, after he made his first in-person appearance before the International Criminal Court (ICC).
output.text: Veronica “Kitty” Duterte on Thursday expressed her support for her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte, after he made his first in-person appearance before the International Criminal Court (ICC). “Conviction, volition and the state of equanimity in any affliction. [L]oud and proud, through and through— forever and always the most unapologetic about you,” Kitty said in a social media post, with an oncoming fist and red heart emojis. Dressed in a black jacket and white button-down polo, Duterte attended the third status conference in his crimes against humanity case as part of preparations for his trial, which is set to begin on November 30. Screenshot from Kitty Duterte IG post Unlike the previous two hearings, Duterte did not waive his appearance. “This is the first time that Mr. Duterte has been in this court. As far as the trial chamber is concerned, if he wishes to leave for any reason, he may do so,” Presiding Judge Joanna Korner said. Some senators expressed their reaction to the former president’s appearance. Senator JV Ejercito said he felt sad seeing Duterte, whom he described as “very frail.” Duterte ally Senator Robin Padilla said he is happy to see the former president but sad at the thought of his condition in the detention facility. Meanwhile, Llore Pasco, whose two sons were killed during Duterte’s war on drugs, said she felt a “sense of relief” that Duterte is being taken care of so that they “can still achieve true justice.” Neri Colmenares, lawyer of alleged drug war victims, said the elder Duterte’s appearance before the ICC status conference indicates that he is capable of understanding the proceedings and is fit to stand trial. Duterte was arrested and taken to The Hague on March 12, 2025. He last appeared before the ICC via video link on March 14, 2025. —Mariel Celine Serquiña/LDF GMA News

output.title: Rodrigo Duterte makes first ICC appearance | ABS-CBN News
output.description: Former President Rodrigo Duterte made his first appearance at the International Criminal Court in The Hague in the Netherlands on Friday, where he faces allegat
output.text: [[PHOTO ALBUM]] MANILA (6th UPDATE) — Former President Rodrigo Duterte made his first appearance at the International Criminal Court in The Hague in the Netherlands on Friday, where he faces allegations of crimes against humanity over his deadly war on drugs. The 79-year-old appeared before judges for a hearing, where he was set to be informed of the crimes he is alleged to have committed, as well as his rights as a defendant. According to ICC spokesperson Fadi el Abdallah on Thursday night, Duterte attended the proceedings via video link. "As Mr Duterte made a long journey ... the Chamber authorised Mr Duterte to follow the hearing at a distance. His counsel, however, is present with us in the courtroom," El Abdallah said. "The suspect is present at the detention center," the spokesperson added. Sounding frail and wearing a blue suit and tie, Duterte spoke briefly to confirm his name and date of birth. The presiding judge allowed him to follow proceedings in absentia due to his long flight to The Hague. Duterte stands accused of the crime against humanity of murder over his years-long campaign against drug users and dealers that rights groups said killed thousands. In the prosecutor's application for his arrest, he said Duterte's alleged crimes were "part of a widespread and systematic attack directed against the civilian population in the Philippines." "Potentially tens of thousands of killings were perpetrated," the prosecutor alleged of the campaign that targeted mostly poor men, often without proof they were linked to drugs. The Philippine National Police has acknowledged more than 6,000 killed in anti-narcotics operation and has claimed those who were killed had violently resisted arrest. Victims' families and rights groups as well as a Department of Justice review have cast doubt on that narrative. They have welcomed the trial as a chance to get justice, while Duterte supporters believe he was "kidnapped" and sent to The Hague amid a spectacular fall-out with the ruling Marcos family. A group of family members, lawyers and human rights activists was set to gather in Manila on Friday night to watch a livestream of the ICC hearing, said organizers Rise Up and the Duterte Accountability Campaign Network. According to international law experts, his whirlwind arrest and surrender to the ICC offers a welcome boon to the embattled court which is being attacked from all sides and sanctioned by the United States. "I see the arrest and handing over of Duterte as a gift at an important moment in time," Willem van Genugten, Professor of International Law at Tilburg University in The Netherlands, told AFP. LAST-MINUTE BID Earlier Friday, his daughter Sara Duterte, vice president of the Philippines, said she had submitted a last-minute bid to get the hearing moved. "We are praying and hoping that the court will grant our request to move the initial appearance just so that we can properly sit down with the former president and discuss the legal strategies since we haven't talked to him yet," she told AFP outside the court. However, ICC Judge Iulia Motoc did not grant the motions of the defense counsel, former executive secretary Salvador Medialdea, to postpone Duterte's appearance hearing to next week. During the initial hearing, Medialdea questioned Duterte's arrest and transfer to The Hague, describing it as an "extrajudicial rendition" and a "kidnapping". He added that he was not given enough time to talk to Duterte regarding the case and the allegations against him, and the former Philippine leader was allegedly not given a hard copy of his arrest warrant. "Two days ago, the whole world has witnessed the degrading fashion in which a former president of a sovereign country was bundled into a private aircraft and summarily transported to the Hague. To us lawyers, this would be called extrajudicial rendition; to the less legally inclined, it was a pure and simple kidnapping. My client was denied all access to the legal recourse in the country of his citizenship and this, all in the nature of political score-settling," Medialdea said. "My client is not able to contribute anything to this hearing. Most importantly, he is not able even to tell you that he has been informed of the charges as contained in the arrest warrant for a reason more pertinent to which I alluded in my written request to this honorable pretrial chamber this morning, and which is confidential in nature," he added. Medialdea also said Duterte was suffering "debilitating medical issues." Duterte appeared sleepy during the proceedings, closing his eyes frequently for long periods. But Judge Motoc told Duterte: "The court doctor was of the opinion that you were fully mentally aware and fit". She set a date of September 23, 2025 for the next stage of the process, a hearing to confirm the charges. INITIAL HEARING At the initial hearing, a suspect can request interim release pending a trial, according to ICC rules. VP Sara, Harry Roque, Robin Padilla arrive at ICC for Rodrigo Duterte's case Following that first hearing, the next phase is a session to confirm the charges, at which point a suspect can challenge the prosecutor's evidence. Only after that hearing will the court decide whether to press ahead with a trial, a process that could take several months or even years. "It's important to underline, as we now start a new stage of proceedings, that Mr. Duterte is presumed innocent," said Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan. In his application for arrest, the prosecutor quoted from some of Duterte's pronouncements when he was running for president. He is cited as saying the number of criminal suspects killed "will become 100,000... I will kill all of you" and the fish in Manila Bay "will become fat because that's where I will throw you." Before he landed in The Hague on Wednesday, Duterte said in a Facebook video: “For all of the whatever happened in the past, ako na ‘yung nag-front sa ating law enforcement pati military. Sinabi ko na, I will protect you and I will… ako ang managot sa lahat.” Duterte case seen as a 'gift' for embattled ICC “This will be a long, legal proceeding but I say to you, I will continue to serve my country and so be it kung ganun ang destiny ko,” the former leader said. Vice President Sara Duterte has labeled her father's arrest as "oppression and persecution". The Duterte family has sought an emergency injunction from the Supreme Court of the Philippines to stop his transfer. Duterte supporters also gathered outside the hulking glass building in the Hague shouting "bring him home." 'NO ONE IS ABOVE THE LAW' But Ecel Sandalo, an anti-Duterte demonstrator, told AFP the fact the former president was on trial had given him "hope that despite all the injustices in the world, there are still small victories that we can celebrate." Victims of the "war on drugs" hope that ex-President Duterte will finally face justice for his alleged crimes. "My clients are very thankful to God because their prayers have been answered," said Gilbert Andres, a lawyer representing victims of the drug war. "The arrest of Rodrigo Duterte is a great signal for international criminal justice. It means that no one is above the law," Andres added. Duterte case seen as a 'gift' for embattled ICC ICC’s Khan hailed Duterte's arrest as a key moment for victims and international justice as a whole. "Many say that international law is not as strong as we want, and I agree with that. But as I also repeatedly emphasize, international law is not as weak as some may think," Khan said in a statement following Duterte's arrival in ICC custody. "When we come together... when we build partnerships, the rule of law can prevail. Warrants can be executed," he said. — With reports from Agence France-Presse
